query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined high‐throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) method integrated with in situ synchrotron X‐ray radiography during rapid pulsed laser melting can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change at melting, and derived liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of high‐entropy alloy (HEA) compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution high-entropy alloys prepared by conventional melting or powder metallurgy, exhibiting homogeneous microstructures prior to melting.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid thermal processing technique using pulsed laser melting that is simultaneously monitored by DSC for thermodynamic signals and in situ synchrotron X‐ray imaging to capture volume and structural evolution during the melting transition.
generation.conditions: Experiments carried out in a controlled, inert atmosphere at ambient pressure with high heating/cooling rates; the method is performed on HEAs with moderate thermal conductivities and minimal pre-melting segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: The transient liquid-phase microstructure and volume expansion differences during rapid melting, which are captured via synchrotron imaging and correlate with calorimetric signals.
generation.mechanism: Rapid pulsed laser heating induces fast melting such that the latent heat effects (enthalpy and entropy of fusion) and concomitant volumetric expansion can be detected by DSC and imaged in real time; the correlation of these measurements allows extraction of both energetic and volume-based thermodynamic properties. The dynamic response mitigates issues with prolonged diffusion or elemental segregation that can obscure melting transitions in conventional DSC.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated method is expected to resolve melting temperatures within an uncertainty of ±5 °C, enthalpy values within ±5% relative error, and capture volume change with a resolution of approximately ±2-3%, enabling extraction of liquid-phase thermodynamic properties over a broad composition space. It should be effective for HEAs that do not exhibit extreme segregation kinetics or overly refractory melting behavior.
generation.baseline: Conventional DSC or static calorimetric methods conducted without in situ imaging, which often face reduced resolution due to slow heating rates and complications from phase segregation.
generation.boundary: Applicability may be limited for HEA systems with very high melting points or severe kinetic limitations (e.g., extreme refractory systems with rapid elemental segregation) where the pulsed laser melting does not produce uniformly measurable thermodynamic signatures.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding how the rapid heating rates might affect the equilibrium melting properties in systems prone to severe undercooling or where laser-induced thermal gradients may cause non-uniform melting. The degree to which these factors can be universally corrected or modeled across all HEA compositions is still uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of HEAs with varying compositions and melting points. For each, perform the proposed pulsed laser melting experiment while simultaneously recording DSC calorimetric data and in situ synchrotron X‐ray images to capture melting temperature, latent heats, and volume changes. Independently, measure these properties using established static DSC and high-resolution dilatometry methods on the same samples. Compare the results across methods.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy (J/g or J/mol) calculated from integrated DSC signal
Fusion entropy (J/(mol·K)) derived from enthalpy and melting temperature
Volume change at melting (%) measured via in situ X‐ray imaging and dilatometry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across multiple HEA compositions, the measurements of melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, or volume change differ consistently by more than approximately ±10% (or exceed the defined resolution limits) from those obtained by conventional methods, the hypothesis that the integrated approach is both accurate and efficient is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
